warmup.q: Two servers' clocks may differ by up to 20 ms. A payment commits on server W with its local clock reading as the commit timestamp, and the client is told "paid". One millisecond later a report on server R reads the account using R's local clock as the snapshot timestamp. What can the report see?
options: Always the payment: it committed before the report started
Possibly the old balance: if R's clock is behind W's, the snapshot timestamp can be lower than the payment's
Half of the payment, because the two servers disagree
Nothing: the read fails with a clock error
warmup.why: Snapshot reads return what committed at or below the snapshot timestamp. If W's clock is ahead, the payment's timestamp can be up to 20 ms above R's reading even though it happened first in real time, so the report misses it. Committing the two rows at one timestamp keeps the report from seeing half a payment; it doesn't make the timestamps agree with real time. That gap is what this lesson's designs close, each at a different price.

sections.h: Distributed SQL stacks four earlier lessons
sections.html:
Move 100 from account A-1001 to merchant account M-2001. The two rows live on different machines, and the database still runs the transfer as one ACID transaction, with no coordination code in the application. Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB and Aurora DSQL do this for SQL, and FoundationDB for a key-value store, though not all of them mean serializable by it (the last section). Every one builds it from four ideas earlier lessons taught, and the figure stacks them.

The first is range sharding, from the Partitioning track. The table's key space is cut into ranges, and each range lives on a few machines. CockroachDB splits a range when it passes 512 MiB, so A-1001 can sit in one range and M-2001 in the next.

The second is a consensus group per range, lesson 4 of this track. Each range is copied to three or five servers by its own Raft group (Paxos in Spanner), with its own leader. A range survives the loss of a server, and its leader puts that range's writes in one order. A cluster runs thousands of these small groups, so leaders spread over every machine.

The third is two-phase commit across ranges, from the Transactions track's atomic commit lesson. The transfer writes provisional values, intents, into both ranges, and then one record decides commit or abort. The Transactions track's worst case was a coordinator that dies and leaves participants in doubt, holding locks. That case disappears here, because the decision record and every intent are themselves writes to Raft groups: they survive the loss of any one machine, and another server can finish the commit.

The fourth is timestamps, from the Faults, time and truth track's lessons on clocks and logical clocks. Each range keeps old versions of its rows (MVCC, from the Transactions track), and a reader takes a snapshot: everything committed at or below timestamp T. That works only if every commit carries a timestamp, and the two rows of one transfer carry the same one. On a single machine a counter does it. Across a thousand machines, who hands out the timestamps, and does a higher timestamp mean later in real time? That one question separates the designs in this lesson, and it decides whether lesson 1's strongest promise, strict serializability, holds. The Try it shows the first three layers in a real CockroachDB 26.3, and the transfer's two rows committed at one timestamp.

try.title: Two ranges, one commit timestamp
steps: Start a single-node CockroachDB 26.3 (about 1 GB) and a helper: docker run -d --name sfz-crdb -m 1g cockroachdb/cockroach:v26.3.5 start-single-node --insecure --cache=128MiB --max-sql-memory=128MiB, then sql() { docker exec -i sfz-crdb ./cockroach sql --insecure -e "$1"; }.
Create the accounts, split the table into two ranges at 'M', and list the ranges with their leaseholder and replicas.

Wait ten seconds, then run the transfer as one transaction and read each row with the hidden column crdb_internal_mvcc_timestamp, the timestamp its version was committed at. Predict: will the two rows, in two ranges, show the same timestamp?
Read the table as it was ten seconds ago with AS OF SYSTEM TIME, then stop: docker rm -f sfz-crdb.

code.title: in any terminal
code.html: sql "CREATE TABLE accounts (id STRING PRIMARY KEY, balance INT NOT NULL);" sql "INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('A-1001', 500), ('M-2001', 0);" sql "ALTER TABLE accounts SPLIT AT VALUES ('M');" sql "SELECT start_key, end_key, range_id, lease_holder, replicas FROM [SHOW RANGES FROM TABLE accounts WITH DETAILS];" sleep 10 sql "BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 'A-1001'; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 'M-2001'; COMMIT;" sql "SELECT id, balance, crdb_internal_mvcc_timestamp FROM accounts;" sql "SELECT id, balance FROM accounts AS OF SYSTEM TIME '-10s';"

The split made two ranges, 87 and 88, each with a leaseholder (the replica that serves reads and leads writes) and a replica set, here just node 1. Both rows of the transfer carry the same commit timestamp although they live in different ranges: two-phase commit stamped them together. The timestamp is a hybrid logical clock value, nanoseconds of wall time before the dot and a logical counter after it. The AS OF SYSTEM TIME read is a snapshot from before the transfer, served from the old versions. Range ids and timestamps differ on your machine. Output trimmed: the statements' own CREATE TABLE, INSERT and COMMIT lines.

sections.h: One server hands out every timestamp: TiDB and FoundationDB
sections.html:
The simplest answer to "who hands out timestamps?" is one server, a timestamp oracle. Google's Percolator (2010) added transactions to Bigtable this way: one machine issued strictly increasing timestamps, about 2 million a second thanks to batching.

TiDB copies Percolator. Its Placement Driver, the small cluster that also tracks where every range lives, hands out a 64-bit timestamp: 46 bits of physical milliseconds and an 18-bit logical counter. The counter advances when two timestamps are needed in the same millisecond, or when the clock steps backwards, so a timestamp never repeats and never goes down. A transaction asks the oracle for a start timestamp, reads the snapshot at it, locks and writes its rows across ranges with two-phase commit over TiKV's Raft groups, then asks the oracle again for a commit timestamp.

Because one server issues every number, the numbers follow real time. If transfer T1 commits before audit T2 starts, T2's start timestamp is higher than T1's commit timestamp, and T2's snapshot includes T1. DDIA calls this a linearizable ID generator, and it is lesson 2's linearizable register in another form. The payment from the warm-up can't be missed.

FoundationDB does the same with a sequencer that hands out commit versions, about a million a second, and adds optimistic concurrency. A transaction reads at a read version and buffers its writes. At commit, resolvers check whether anything it read was overwritten since its read version, and abort it if so. The result is strict serializability without locks. The resolvers keep only five seconds of history in memory, so a transaction that runs longer than five seconds is rejected; FoundationDB's authors say that hitting the limit usually means a client is doing reads one at a time.

The price is the oracle itself. Every transaction makes one or two round trips to it before it can commit, and it is one leader, replicated for failover but not spread out. In one region that adds a fraction of a millisecond. With servers in two regions, a transaction far from the oracle pays a cross-region round trip, about 70 ms, for each timestamp. TiDB's default transaction mode is pessimistic, with locks taken as rows are written, and its REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation under a MySQL name, so it allows write skew. Spanner set out to remove the oracle altogether.

sections.h: Spanner waits out the clock's error before it answers
sections.html:
Spanner (Google, 2012) has no oracle. Each server stamps commits from its own clock. The Faults, time and truth track showed why that is dangerous: clocks disagree, and a reading says nothing about its own error. Spanner's fix is an API that reports the error. TrueTime returns an interval, TT.now() = [earliest, latest], and guarantees that the true time is inside it. GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every data centre keep the interval narrow. In the 2012 paper, ε, half its width, grew in a sawtooth from about 1 to 7 ms over each 30-second poll of the time masters, so about 4 ms most of the time, with spikes when a time master or the network misbehaved. Google hasn't published newer figures; the "generally less than 10 ms" often quoted is the same paper's own summary.

A read-write transaction takes locks, runs two-phase commit across the Paxos groups of the ranges it touched, and its coordinator picks a commit timestamp no lower than TT.now().latest. Then comes the rule that gives the design its name, commit wait: the coordinator releases no locks and tells no one about the commit until TT.now().earliest has passed the timestamp. Because the timestamp was picked at the top of an interval and the wait ends when the bottom reaches it, the wait is about 2ε. The stepper walks through it with ε = 10 ms.

When the client hears "committed", the commit timestamp is in the past on every clock. Any transaction that starts afterwards reads at TT.now().latest, which is at or above the true time, so its timestamp is higher and its snapshot includes the commit. Spanner calls this external consistency; lesson 1 called it strict serializability.

The wait would hurt if it came on top of everything else, so Spanner overlaps it with the Paxos replication of the commit record. The 2012 paper measured commit wait at about 5 ms next to about 9 ms of Paxos latency, and a mean write latency of about 14 ms with one, three or five replicas. Strong reads pay a little too. A read at TT.now().latest may have to wait until its replicas are sure no transaction can still commit below that timestamp, which the lab models as a read that waits on an intent. Smaller ε means less waiting, which is why Google built the clock hardware in the first place.

Spanner's default stays serializable. It now also offers REPEATABLE READ, which is snapshot isolation, set per client or per transaction, for workloads where reads blocking behind writes cost more than the occasional write skew.

frames.say: Now the same two servers trusting their clocks. The settlement server commits at what its clock read when it started, s = 10, and answers at 8 ms. At 9 ms the auditor reads at what its clock says, -1. The batch was paid before the audit began, and the audit doesn't see it: a stale read, caused only by 20 ms of disagreement between two clocks. The lab's trust scenario prints this run.

With commit wait the transaction was decided at 8 ms but announced at 20 ms, 2ε after it picked s = 20, and the audit's timestamp, 21, came out above it. Trusting the clocks answered 12 ms sooner and the audit missed a batch that was already paid, though it still saw both ranges agree. With commitwait 3, 2ε is 6 ms, less than the 8 ms the commit needs anyway, so the client is told at 8 ms: the wait hides entirely behind replication.

sections.h: CockroachDB moves the uncertainty from writers to readers
sections.html:
CockroachDB runs on ordinary servers with NTP and no special clocks, so a 2ε commit wait on every write would be large. It takes two ideas instead.

The first is a hybrid logical clock, from the Faults, time and truth track's logical clocks lesson. A node's timestamp is its wall time plus a logical counter, and a node that receives a higher timestamp in a message moves its own clock up to it. Causally related events therefore always get increasing timestamps, even between nodes whose clocks disagree. The Try it in the first section showed one: wall nanoseconds, a dot, then the counter.

The second is a promised bound on clock disagreement, the max offset, 500 ms by default (Cockroach Labs suggests 250 ms for new multi-region clusters). The bound is enforced: a node whose clock is off from at least half of the other nodes by 80% of the max offset shuts itself down rather than serve wrong answers.

Writers don't wait at all. A read at timestamp T knows that any value with a timestamp above T + max offset was written after it began, whatever the clocks say. A value between T and T + max offset is in the read's uncertainty interval: it may have committed before the read started, on a node whose clock runs ahead. The read can't skip it, so it moves its own timestamp up past that value. If its earlier reads are still valid at the new timestamp, it carries on; otherwise the transaction restarts with a ReadWithinUncertaintyIntervalError. The top of the interval doesn't move with the timestamp, so restarts must end. The cost lands only on reads of recently written keys, and only on those within the max offset of a write, instead of on every write.

Writes are intents with a transaction record, as in section 1. Parallel commits set the record to STAGING while the intents are still being replicated; the transaction counts as committed once every intent has reached consensus, so commit takes one round of consensus instead of two, and the intents are cleaned up afterwards.

The guarantee is serializable by default, though not strict serializable: CockroachDB's docs say clock skew beyond the max offset can break single-key linearizability between causally dependent transactions. READ COMMITTED is also available, with a fresh snapshot per statement, no read refresh and no serialization retries, at the price of lost updates and write skew. YugabyteDB works the same way: hybrid time, a 500 ms default bound that stops servers beyond it, and an option to take the bound from AWS's ClockBound daemon instead, which on AWS is typically well under a millisecond.

try.title: Restart above a value you can't place
steps: Run the restart scenario: the same two servers, the same transaction and audit as the last Try it, with CockroachDB's policy: the writer commits at its clock, and the reader's window reaches 2ε above its own clock.
Find the read timestamp, the top of its window and the timestamp it restarts at. How long did the client wait for its commit this time, and how long the audit?
Run restart 1: with clocks within 1 ms, is the batch inside the window?

try.expect:
RESTART, clocks within 10 ms of true time: settle runs 10 ms ahead, audit-0 10 ms behind
t=    0  settle   batch 1: commit timestamp 10 (its clock reads 10)
t=    4  settle   intents for batch 1 written to payouts and ledger at 10
t=    8  settle   commit record replicated: batch 1 is decided
t=    8  settle   client told: batch 1 is paid (8 ms)
t=    9  audit-0  audit starts: read timestamp -1 (clock -1), uncertain up to 19
t=   11  audit-0  finds a version it can't place: restarts at 10
t=   13  audit-0  reads payouts = 1, ledger = 1
fresh: the audit sees batch 1 (1 restart(s), waited 0 ms)

The writer answered at 8 ms, as fast as trusting the clocks. The audit read at -1, but its window reached 19 (2ε above its clock, the most two clocks can disagree), and the batch's timestamp 10 fell inside it. So it restarted at 10 and saw the batch: one extra round trip, 4 ms in all instead of 2. With restart 1 the window is 2 ms wide and the clocks barely disagree, so the batch's timestamp is already below the read timestamp: no restart.

sections.h: Aurora DSQL coordinates once at commit, and what each design costs
sections.html:
Aurora DSQL (AWS, generally available since May 2025) makes a different trade: optimistic concurrency at snapshot isolation only. A transaction reads at its start time from multi-version storage, with no locks and no coordination; storage waits until it has applied every commit at or below that time. Writes stay in the query processor until COMMIT. Then an adjudicator checks whether another transaction wrote the same keys since this one started. If one did, the later one fails with SQLSTATE 40001 and code OC000, and the application retries. The commit is final once DSQL's journal stores it. That is one coordination step per transaction, at commit, and no deadlocks, since nothing waits on a lock; SELECT ... FOR UPDATE simply counts as a write when the adjudicator checks.

The limits come with the design. Snapshot isolation is PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ, so write skew is possible: two doctors can still both go off call. A transaction may change at most 3,000 rows and 10 MiB and may run at most 5 minutes. And a hot key, such as a merchant's balance row that every payment updates, turns into a retry loop, because every writer but one fails at commit.

So "distributed SQL" doesn't mean "serializable". Spanner and CockroachDB default to serializable and now offer weaker levels; TiDB and YugabyteDB default to snapshot isolation; Aurora DSQL offers nothing else. Read the isolation level in the docs, not the marketing.

Here is where each design charges for the same transfer, with a consensus round inside one region of about 1 to 2 ms:

System Commit timestamp from A write pays A read pays Default isolation
TiDB an oracle (the Placement Driver) two oracle trips, 2PC over Raft one oracle trip snapshot (RR), pessimistic
FoundationDB a sequencer a version, a resolver check a read version strict serializable (OCC)
Spanner TrueTime commit wait of about 2ε, overlapped with Paxos may wait for safe time serializable (external consistency)
CockroachDB hybrid clock, max offset one consensus round (parallel commits) a restart if a value is uncertain serializable
Aurora DSQL adjudicators at commit one adjudication, one journal write nothing extra snapshot only

All of them pay a consensus round per write and some coordination per transaction, where one PostgreSQL primary pays an fsync. You buy that for data that outgrows a machine, or for a database that survives losing a region. The Try it measures the clock part on its own.

Restarts cost writes nothing and add about one round trip to the audits that meet a fresh value. Here that is most audits, because every auditor reads the one key the job rewrites every 10 to 20 ms: the worst case, where a real table spreads its reads over many keys. Trusting the clocks is the fastest and, from ε = 5 ms up, wrong more often than you would ship. The run is seeded, so these numbers are exact.

refs.title: Aurora DSQL: Cluster quotas and database limits
Brooker: DSQL Vignette, Transactions and Durability

analogy: Think of three bank branches in different time zones, each stamping deposit slips with its own wall clock. A timestamp oracle is a head office that issues every slip number by phone: always in order, and every branch waits on the line. Spanner gives each branch a clock certified to within a few seconds and makes the clerk hold every slip until that many seconds have passed, so no later slip anywhere can carry a smaller stamp. CockroachDB lets clerks stamp at once and makes an auditor who finds a slip stamped just after the start of the audit start over, counting it in. The analogy breaks on scale: real clocks drift by milliseconds, not seconds, and the waiting and restarting happen thousands of times a second, which is why a few milliseconds of clock error turn into a visible cost.
world: Your payments database is most likely one Oracle or PostgreSQL primary with a standby, and for a ledger that fits on one machine that is still the cheapest way to get serializable, linearizable writes: one fsync and no clocks to trust. Distributed SQL earns its cost when the ledger outgrows the machine or must keep taking payments when a region is lost. If you move, three habits carry over from this lesson. Retry on SQLSTATE 40001, because CockroachDB's restarts and DSQL's commit-time conflicts both surface there, and make the retried transaction idempotent with the same keys you send the card issuer. Check the isolation level you actually get: DSQL and YugabyteDB's defaults are snapshot isolation, not the serializable your Oracle code may assume. And keep hot rows such as a merchant's running balance out of the hot path, because optimistic systems turn them into retry storms.
mistake: The common mistake is assuming "distributed SQL" means "serializable and always up to date". Teams port code that relies on serializable isolation to a system whose default is snapshot isolation (Aurora DSQL, YugabyteDB, TiDB's REPEATABLE READ) and get write skew they never saw before, or they run CockroachDB with clocks they never monitor and assume real-time order. It happens because the SQL looks the same and the product pages say ACID. The fix is to read the isolation level and the clock assumptions in the docs, set the level explicitly per transaction, monitor clock offset (CockroachDB and YugabyteDB will stop a node that drifts, which is an outage you should see coming), and handle retries with SQLSTATE 40001 in one place.

compare.title: One transfer's commit path in Spanner and in CockroachDB

a.label: Spanner
a.title: TrueTime and commit wait
a.html:
1  lock A-1001 and M-2001 (two-phase locking)
2  prepare in both Paxos groups
3  s = TT.now().latest
4  replicate the commit record   (Paxos)
5  wait until TT.now().earliest > s
   (about 2 x epsilon, overlapped with 4)
6  release locks, tell the client

readers: read at TT.now().latest,
         may wait for safe time

b.label: CockroachDB
b.title: hybrid clock and uncertainty
b.html:
1  ts = HLC.now() at the gateway node
2  write intents in both Raft groups
   and set the record to STAGING
   (parallel commits: one round)
3  tell the client once all are replicated
4  resolve the intents afterwards

readers: value in (T, T + max offset]?
         move T above it, refresh
         or restart

compare.note: Both make a transaction's timestamp agree with real time, and both depend on a bound on clock error. Spanner makes every writer wait out its bound, which is small because of special hardware, so readers never doubt a timestamp. CockroachDB's bound is large (500 ms by default) because it runs on ordinary clocks, so making writers wait would be too slow; it lets readers find the doubtful values and pay only when they hit one. Which costs less depends on the clock and on how often reads touch freshly written keys.

worked.title: Size the clock tax for three kinds of clock

steps.say: Write the two costs as formulas. With every clock within ε of true time, two clocks differ by up to 2ε. Commit wait adds what the wait doesn't hide behind replication; an uncertainty window catches values written up to 2ε after a read's clock.
steps.code:
commitWait(eps, replicationMs) = max(0, 2 * eps - replicationMs)
windowMs(eps)                  = 2 * eps   // CockroachDB: --max-offset

steps.say: AWS's Time Sync Service with the Nitro hardware clock reports error bounds under 40 µs. The wait vanishes behind a 1 ms consensus round, and the window is tiny.
steps.code:
eps = 0.04 ms, replication 1 ms
commit wait  = max(0, 0.08 - 1) = 0 ms
window       = 0.08 ms

steps.say: Spanner's 2012 numbers: ε about 4 ms (peaks near 7), Paxos about 9 ms. The formula says the wait could hide entirely, yet the paper's one-replica benchmark took 14.4 ms per write with commit wait and 9.4 ms without: about 5 ms added. Overlap hides part of the wait, not all of it, so treat the formula as a lower bound.
steps.code:
eps = 4 ms (peaks 7), replication about 9 ms
formula: max(0, 8 - 9)  = 0 ms
measured: 14.4 - 9.4    = about 5 ms

steps.say: Public internet NTP, tens of ms of error. Commit wait would add most of a 100 ms window to every write, so this is CockroachDB's territory: no wait, and reads of keys written in the last few hundred ms may restart.
steps.code:
eps = 50 ms, replication 2 ms
commit wait  = max(0, 100 - 2) = 98 ms per write
window       = 100 ms (CockroachDB default max offset: 500 ms)

steps.say: The lesson in code: the bound, not the clock reading, sets the price. A Kotlin check you could put in a startup probe, using the same numbers.
steps.code: fun commitWaitMs(epsMs: Double, replicationMs: Double) = maxOf(0.0, 2 * epsMs - replicationMs) listOf(0.04, 4.0, 50.0).forEach { eps -> println("eps $eps ms -> wait ${commitWaitMs(eps, 2.0)} ms, window ${2 * eps} ms") } // eps 0.04 ms -> wait 0.0 ms, window 0.08 ms // eps 4.0 ms -> wait 6.0 ms, window 8.0 ms // eps 50.0 ms -> wait 98.0 ms, window 100.0 ms

lab.title: Commit timestamps on clocks that disagree
steps: Read Clocks.kt (a clock with an offset it doesn't know, and a TrueTime interval around it) and the provided half of Transactions.kt: settle runs the two-range transaction, and checkedAudit marks an audit stale or fractured. Processes are plain Kotlin that call sim.sleep; virtual time makes ten seconds of traffic run in milliseconds. Run the tests once: all 14 fail.
Write Range.read in Mvcc.kt: an intent at or below the window's top blocks, a committed version inside the window is uncertain, otherwise return the snapshot value. The three RangeTest tests pass.
Write commitTimestamp and commitWait: the clock, or TrueTime's latest followed by a wait until TrueTime's earliest reaches the timestamp. The commit-wait test passes with exactly 20 ms.

Write audit: pick the read timestamp and window for the policy, then loop: one round trip, read both ranges, wait 1 ms on an intent, restart above an uncertain value. The remaining tests pass, including a property test over hundreds of seeds and bounds: commit wait and restarts never give a stale or fractured audit.
hints: In Range.read, check intents before uncertainty: an intent you skip could commit at a timestamp below yours a moment later, and a reader that ignores it can see one range's half of a transfer and not the other's.
For RESTART the window is readTs + 2 * epsilonMs, because the writer's clock may be ε ahead of true time while yours is ε behind.
When you restart, move readTs up to the uncertain timestamp but leave the window's top where it was. A window that moved with the read could find a new uncertain value on every attempt.
A wait on an intent sleeps 1 ms with no new round trip; a restart costs rttMs. The exact-latency tests depend on that difference.

drill.title: Write the read rule from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write read(key, readTs, limit) for one MVCC range: block on an intent at or below the limit, report the highest committed timestamp in (readTs, limit] as uncertain, and otherwise return the newest committed version at or below readTs.

answer.html: fun read(key: String, readTs: Long, limit: Long): ReadResult { val all = versionsOf(key) all.firstOrNull { !it.committed && it.ts <= limit } ?.let { return Blocked(it.txn!!) } // may commit below us: wait all.filter { it.committed && it.ts > readTs && it.ts <= limit } .maxOfOrNull { it.ts } ?.let { return Uncertain(it) } // can't tell before from after val v = all.filter { it.committed && it.ts <= readTs }.maxBy { it.ts } return Value(v.value, v.ts) // the snapshot at readTs }

recap: Distributed SQL stacks range sharding, a Raft or Paxos group per range, two-phase commit across ranges with intents and a replicated transaction record, and MVCC commit timestamps.
The timestamps decide the guarantee. A timestamp oracle (Percolator, TiDB's Placement Driver, FoundationDB's sequencer) follows real time but costs a round trip to one leader per transaction.

Spanner's TrueTime reports [earliest, latest]; a transaction commits at latest and waits about 2ε until earliest passes it, overlapped with Paxos. That buys external consistency (strict serializability).

CockroachDB uses hybrid clocks and a max offset (500 ms default) and lets readers restart above values in their uncertainty window; parallel commits make a commit one consensus round. Serializable, not strictly.

Aurora DSQL is optimistic snapshot isolation with one adjudication at commit, 40001 on conflict and limits of 3,000 rows, 10 MiB and 5 minutes. Distributed SQL doesn't mean serializable: check the level.

explain.prompt: Explain why a distributed SQL database can't just stamp each commit with the local clock of the server that coordinates it, and two ways real systems avoid the problem.
explain.answer: A snapshot read returns everything committed at or below its timestamp. If each server uses its own clock and clocks disagree, a payment committed on a server whose clock runs fast can carry a timestamp above that of a report started later on a server whose clock runs slow, so the report misses a payment that was already confirmed: a stale read, even though each transaction was atomic. Spanner avoids it with TrueTime, which reports an interval that surely contains the true time: it commits at the top of the interval and waits, about twice the clock error, until the bottom has passed that timestamp before telling anyone, so every later transaction gets a higher timestamp. CockroachDB avoids it without special clocks: it promises a maximum offset between clocks, kills nodes that exceed it, and makes a reader that meets a value just above its own timestamp, within that offset, move its timestamp up or restart. A third way is a single timestamp oracle, as in TiDB, at the price of a round trip to one server.

deeper.html:
Percolator's cleanup. Percolator commits by rewriting one primary lock; secondary locks point at it. A reader that finds a lock left by a crashed client checks the primary and rolls the transaction forward or back. That lazy cleanup could delay commits by tens of seconds: fine for building a search index, which was its job, and far too slow for a payment.

Deterministic databases. Calvin (2012) agrees on the order of whole transactions first, through a replicated log, and then every replica runs them in that order with no two-phase commit at all, at the price of declaring a transaction's reads and writes up front. FaunaDB built on the idea, and Cassandra 6.0's Accord, still alpha, orders multi-partition transactions without a leader.

Better clocks for everyone. AWS's Time Sync Service gives EC2 instances an error bound under 100 µs over NTP and under 40 µs through the Nitro hardware clock, and its ClockBound daemon reports [earliest, latest] like TrueTime. YugabyteDB can use it. As cloud clocks improve, commit wait and uncertainty windows shrink toward the cost of a consensus round, and the designs in this lesson converge.

Reading further. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, covers distributed transactions in chapter 8 and timestamps, linearizable ID generators and consensus in chapter 10.
